1. The frames show a large grid of identical small houses, with the front houses and then more and more of the grid lighting up. The caption names the data sources as FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It also says "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast". The idea seems to be a share or count of homes, or of households, passing some threshold. The picture doesn't say which threshold. It could be homes that are affordable, or homes where buying beats renting.

2. In frame 1 the houses are almost all dark grey. From frame 3 on, a bright wave spreads from the front-left corner across the grid. By frames 5 and 6 most of the grid is lit, and only the back-right section stays dark. The houses themselves don't change, and neither does the camera.

3. A growing fraction of the housing stock gets "highlighted" as time passes, but the frames don't say what the highlight stands for. The sources suggest it ties home prices, rents and mortgage rates together. There are no numbers, labels, legend or axis, so I can't say whether lit means "cheaper to buy", "cheaper to rent" or something else. I also can't say what the time span is.

4. No concrete advice comes out of the frames. The only guidance is the cautionary text: this is illustrative, US-only history and not a forecast. A viewer shouldn't use it to decide whether to rent or buy, and it doesn't answer your question about whether renting costs more than buying once you count interest, tax, insurance and repairs.

5. The on-screen text gave that caution, "history, not a forecast", and nothing else. Any buy-or-rent conclusion would be my own, not the animation's, so I'm not drawing one.
